identification.summary: UAT-9244 is Cisco Talos's designation for a China-nexus advanced persistent threat cluster that Talos disclosed on 2026-03-05 [S1]. Talos assesses with high confidence that it is closely associated with FamousSparrow and overlaps with Tropic Trooper [S1][S2]. Talos reports it has targeted telecommunications infrastructure in South America since 2024, across Windows and Linux endpoints and edge devices [S1][S2]. It uses three implants: TernDoor (Windows), PeerTime (Linux/embedded) and BruteEntry (edge-device scanner/relay) [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Talos could not establish a firm link to Salt Typhoon despite overlapping targeting [S2][S4]. ESET documents FamousSparrow as a China-aligned group [S6]; do not merge Talos, Microsoft and ESET cluster boundaries. One report says TernDoor has been used since at least November 2024 [S4]. The Hacker News lists PeerTime under the name 'angrypeer' [S2].

attribution.sponsor: China-nexus (no specific state organization named in sources reviewed)
attribution.confidence: Cisco Talos: high confidence that UAT-9244 is closely associated with FamousSparrow and overlaps with Tropic Trooper [S1][S2]
attribution.basis: Talos cites overlapping tooling, TTPs and victimology with FamousSparrow/Tropic Trooper [S1]. TernDoor is described as a variant of the previously disclosed CrowDoor malware [S2][S4]. PeerTime debug strings are in Simplified Chinese, which Talos treats as an indicator of Chinese-speaking operators [S5]. This is a vendor assessment, not government attribution.

objectives: Reporting characterizes the activity as espionage-oriented, aimed at persistent access to telecommunications networks, with remote command execution, lateral movement and relay infrastructure; no destructive or ransomware activity was described [S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Targets include Windows and Linux endpoints and edge devices of telecom providers [S1][S2]. Specific victim organizations and countries were not identified in the sources I could review [S1].

capabilities.summary: TernDoor is a Windows backdoor derived from CrowDoor; it is delivered via DLL side-loading (benign wsprint.exe loads malicious BugSplatRc64.dll, which decrypts a data file and runs it in memory), reportedly injects into msiexec.exe, persists via scheduled task or Registry Run key, and embeds a driver able to suspend, resume and terminate processes [S4]. PeerTime is a Linux ELF backdoor that uses the BitTorrent protocol for peer-based C2 and payload retrieval, with builds for ARM, MIPS, PowerPC and AArch64, in C/C++ and Rust variants, deployed by a shell script with an 'instrumentor' binary that checks for Docker [S5]. BruteEntry is a Go-based tool that registers with C2, receives IP lists, and turns compromised edge devices into Operational Relay Boxes that brute-force SSH, Postgres and Tomcat servers [S1][S5]. Initial access vector is not known from reviewed sources; the associated lineage has previously exploited outdated Windows Server and Exchange Server to drop web shells [S4].

campaigns.name: TernDoor use
campaigns.summary: One report states TernDoor has been in use since at least November 2024 [S4].

campaigns.name: Talos public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Cisco Talos published its report on UAT-9244 describing TernDoor, PeerTime and BruteEntry [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: China-nexus cluster UAT-9244, closely associated with FamousSparrow and overlapping Tropic Trooper per Talos [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: TernDoor, PeerTime and BruteEntry cross-platform implants, with DLL side-loading, an embedded process-control driver, BitTorrent-based C2 and ORB creation [S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised edge devices used as Operational Relay Boxes and proxy nodes; BitTorrent peer network for PeerTime C2 [S1][S5]. Specific domains and certificates were not verified in sources I could open.
diamond.technology: Windows hosts, Linux servers, and embedded/edge devices (ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, AArch64), with SSH, Postgres and Tomcat services as brute-force targets [S5].

gaps: Cisco Talos primary report could not be opened (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage, so validate against the primary document [S1].
Initial access vector, victim countries/organizations and dwell times are not identified in reviewed sources.
Infrastructure indicators (e.g., domains, shared SSL certificates) were not verified.
Relationship to Salt Typhoon is unresolved: Talos could not confirm a link, the FamousSparrow-Salt Typhoon relationship was not verified [S2][S6].
The Tropic Trooper overlap is stated by Talos; independent corroboration was not found.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID and no Microsoft name identified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the operational environment includes telecom provider networks, whose edge devices (routers, appliances) and Linux/Windows servers are the observed terrain [S1][S5]. Step 3-4: adversary most likely course of action is continued persistent access to telecom providers with lateral movement and use of compromised edge devices as relay boxes to scan or brute-force further targets [S1][S3]; a more dangerous course would be use of that access and ORB network against third-party networks routed through compromised carriers (inference, not stated in sources). Candidate indicators: wsprint.exe loading BugSplatRc64.dll, msiexec.exe injection, scheduled-task/Run-key persistence, unexpected BitTorrent traffic from edge devices, outbound SSH/Postgres/Tomcat brute-force from infrastructure devices, ELF binaries on ARM/MIPS devices [S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share Talos-reported behaviors with partners operating or relying on South American telecom links, noting that edge devices may be both victims and attack relays [S1][S5]. Authorities: monitoring of commercial/partner carrier infrastructure depends on partner agreements and host-nation authority; coordinate through established cyber threat-sharing channels. Mission assurance: identify mission dependencies on affected carriers and plan alternate paths and integrity checks on edge devices. Coordination: confirm indicators with the primary Talos report before tasking collection or defensive action.
